script.opening: (Embarrassed, avoids eye contact, speaks quietly.) "This is really embarrassing, doctor, but — there was blood when I ejaculated, a couple of times this week. I've been up at night googling it and I've completely convinced myself it's cancer. I'm only 33 but I'm terrified. Is it? I haven't been able to think about anything else."

facts.text: "Twice this week. Pinkish-red, I suppose." If asked: "Yes, it was definitely the semen" — not in the urine. First time ever.
"No, none of that" — no pain or burning passing urine, no blood in urine, no frequency or difficulty, no discharge.
"No lumps, no injury, nothing like that." No pain in the testicles, perineum or back. No recent procedures.
"No. I feel completely fine otherwise" — no fever, weight loss, night sweats, bruising or bleeding elsewhere. No blood thinners. No regular medicines, no allergies. BP never checked.
If asked sensitively: "Nothing I'm worried about. But test me if it helps." One female partner for 3 years, monogamous; condoms not used. No partner symptoms.
Accountant, lives with his partner, Esi. Non-smoker, drinks 8 units a week. Cycles to work. Dad is 64 and well; no family history of prostate cancer.
"Prostate cancer, mainly. Every page seemed to mention it. I haven't slept properly for days."

Anxious and embarrassed. Relaxes if the doctor normalises it. Wants a straight answer: "Yes. That's all I want." Surprised: "Really? The websites made it sound so serious." Asks: "And if it keeps happening?" Happy to come in tomorrow for an examination and urine tests. If dismissed without any assessment, stays worried.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror of prostate cancer from late-night googling; embarrassment; not sleeping.

cues: "I've been up at night googling." — ask what he read.
"I'm only 33." — age matters; use it in reassurance.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that in a YOUNG man (<40) with a short episode and no red flags, haematospermia is almost always BENIGN/self-limiting — and reassures proportionately after assessment rather than over-investigating

Takes a targeted history (duration/recurrence, urinary symptoms, haematuria, STI risk/discharge, recent procedures, trauma, anticoagulants, fever, weight loss/bone pain) and considers the benign causes (idiopathic, prostatitis/urethritis, STI, post-procedure)

Examines appropriately — arranges an in-person examination (not possible on video): BP, urine dip/MSU, STI screen if indicated, external genitalia — with DRE/PSA guided by age and findings (more selective in a low-risk young man; PSA not within 48 hours of ejaculation)

Knows the features warranting INVESTIGATION/REFERRAL — age ≥40 (especially persistent/recurrent), haematuria, abnormal (hard/nodular) prostate or raised PSA, systemic red flags — and that NICE NG12 uses a suspected cancer pathway referral for a PSA above the age-specific range or a malignant-feeling prostate, with separate haematuria and testicular routes

Manages the low-risk patient: treats any identified infection, gives clear reassurance, and SAFETY-NETS for persistence/recurrence, haematuria, urinary/systemic symptoms or age threshold prompting later investigation

Addresses the cancer FEAR directly and proportionately — acknowledging the anxiety/embarrassment and the googling — with honest reassurance grounded in assessment, neither dismissive nor falsely alarming
Normalises the symptom, explains the reasoning in accessible terms, and checks understanding so the reassurance lands

Safety-nets and follows up: which features warrant return/investigation (persistence, haematuria, systemic symptoms, age), treatment of any cause, and review — proportionate reassurance for the young/low-risk, clear threshold to investigate the older/red-flag patient

worked.txt: "There’s no need to be embarrassed — this is a common thing to come about, and I’m really glad you did rather than worrying alone. Let me ask a few things, and arrange to examine you in person, and then I can give you a proper, honest answer rather than the internet’s worst-case version."

"Any pain passing urine, blood in your wee, discharge, recent injury, or new sexual partners? Any fevers, weight loss? … None. I can’t check your blood pressure or examine you over video, so let’s book you in to do that and test your urine — and depending on that, possibly a prostate check, though at your age that’s less likely to be needed."

"Here’s the honest reassurance you came for: in a man of 33, with no other symptoms, blood in the semen is almost always harmless and settles on its own — often from a tiny blood vessel or mild inflammation. Cancer is a very uncommon cause at your age."
"If your urine test or swabs show an infection, I’ll treat that. Otherwise there’s usually nothing that needs doing — it tends to clear by itself over a few weeks."

worked.lbl: Be clear when it WOULD matter
worked.txt: "So you know where the line is: I’d want to look further if it keeps happening over several weeks, if you see blood in your wee, get urinary symptoms or feel unwell — or, in older men, it’s checked more thoroughly. But none of that applies to you right now."

"Try to step away from the 2am googling — it’s feeding the fear. If it persists, recurs, or any of those warning signs appear, come back and we’ll investigate properly. But I’m genuinely reassuring, not fobbing you off."

f.learning: Haematospermia (blood in the ejaculate) is managed by AGE and red flags. In men UNDER 40 with a single or short episode and no red flags it is almost always BENIGN and self-limiting — commonly idiopathic, or due to inflammation/infection (prostatitis, urethritis, STI), recent instrumentation/prostate biopsy, vigorous sexual activity, or minor vessel bleeding — with cancer an uncommon cause, so strong, honest reassurance is appropriate after a sensible assessment. Take a targeted history (duration/recurrence, urinary symptoms, haematuria, STI risk/discharge, recent procedures, trauma, anticoagulants, fever, weight loss/bone pain), check BP (severe hypertension is associated), dip the urine/MSU, screen for STIs if indicated, and examine the external genitalia in person (a video consultation cannot do this), with DRE and PSA guided by age and findings (important in the older/persistent patient, more selective in a low-risk young man; PSA not within 48 hours of ejaculation or vigorous exercise, per the GOV.UK Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme). Recognise the features that warrant INVESTIGATION/REFERRAL: age ≥40 (especially persistent or recurrent), associated visible/non-visible haematuria, an abnormal (hard/nodular) prostate, a raised age-adjusted PSA, or systemic red flags — these raise concern for PROSTATE cancer or other urological pathology, and NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) uses a suspected cancer pathway referral for a PSA above the age-specific range (40–49 above 2.5, 50–59 above 3.5, 60–69 above 4.5, 70–79 above 6.5 µg/L) or a malignant-feeling prostate, with separate routes for visible haematuria at 45+ (or non-visible at 60+ with dysuria or raised white cells) and for a testicular change. For the low-risk young man, treat any identified infection, give clear proportionate reassurance, and safety-net for persistence/recurrence, haematuria, urinary/systemic symptoms or reaching the age threshold. The communication core is the cancer FEAR fuelled by googling: acknowledge it, reassure honestly and proportionately (usually benign, rarely cancer in the young), and keep the threshold to investigate clear for the older/persistent/red-flag scenario — neither dismissive nor falsely alarming.

knowledge.summary: Blood in the semen in a man under 40, with no other symptoms, is almost always benign and settles on its own. Assess sensibly, test for infection, check blood pressure, reassure honestly, and be clear about the features that would change the plan.

points.t: Most cases in men under 40 have no identifiable cause or follow inflammation or infection (prostatitis, urethritis, sexually transmitted infection), recent instrumentation or prostate biopsy, or minor vessel bleeding. Cancer is an uncommon cause in this group. EAU [2] (international): men over 40, those with persistent or recurrent haemospermia, and those with associated haematuria or other symptoms are the higher-risk groups.

Number of episodes and duration; is it definitely semen (not urine, not the partner’s bleeding); urinary symptoms, visible haematuria, discharge, testicular pain or lump; sexual health risk; recent procedures or trauma; bleeding elsewhere, anticoagulants; fever, weight loss, bone pain; travel to areas where schistosomiasis is common.

Blood pressure (severe hypertension is a recognised association); urine dip and MSU; first-void urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea if there is any sexual risk; examination of the external genitalia in person. DRE and PSA are selective in a low-risk man under 40 and routine for men over 40 or with persistent symptoms.

NICE NG12 [1]: refer on a suspected cancer pathway if PSA is above the age-specific reference range (40–49 above 2.5, 50–59 above 3.5, 60–69 above 4.5, 70–79 above 6.5 µg/L; clinical judgement under 40) or the prostate feels malignant on DRE. GOV.UK PCRMP [3]: no ejaculation or vigorous exercise in the 48 hours before the test, and not within 6 weeks of a prostate biopsy; defer if there is active urinary infection.

NICE NG12 [1]: visible haematuria at 45 or over, or non-visible haematuria at 60 or over with dysuria or a raised white cell count, triggers the bladder or kidney route. A non-painful testicular swelling or change in shape or texture triggers the testicular route.

Treat a confirmed STI per the relevant BASHH guideline (for example the BASHH chlamydia guideline, 2026) and arrange partner notification. If symptoms suggest acute prostatitis, NICE NG110 [4] applies. Otherwise no treatment is needed; most episodes resolve without intervention.

Persistent or recurrent haematospermia, associated haematuria, abnormal prostate or raised age-specific PSA, a testicular lump, or systemic features: refer to urology (suspected cancer pathway where NICE NG12 criteria are met).

You said you’ve convinced yourself it’s cancer. What have you read that’s made you think that?

That sounds exhausting. So what you’re hoping for today is a straight answer on whether this could be cancer?

model.text: Yes. That’s all I want.

Really? The websites made it sound so serious.

model.text: Here’s what I suggest. Drop a urine sample at the surgery so we can check for infection and blood, and a first-pass urine sample to test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. I’d like your blood pressure checked, and a quick examination of your testicles in person with a doctor. A prostate test isn’t usually needed at your age unless something else turns up.

model.text: I can do that tomorrow.
Great. If anything shows infection, I’ll treat it. If it’s all normal, there’s nothing more to do except let it settle.
And if it keeps happening?

Good question. If it keeps happening over the next few weeks, or you see blood in your urine, get pain or a lump in the testicles, fevers, or feel generally unwell, come back. Then I’d look further, with a prostate check and blood test, and possibly a referral to the urology team.
That makes sense.

One more thing. The late-night googling is feeding the fear. If you catch yourself doing it, remind yourself of what we agreed: tests tomorrow, and I’ll ring you with the results. Can you tell me back what you’re going to do?
Urine samples and blood pressure and the examination tomorrow. You’ll call with results. Come back if it keeps happening or I see blood in my wee, pain, a lump or fever.
Exactly. And if you ever can’t pass urine at all, or feel very unwell with a high temperature, get seen the same day.

social.t: Late-night searching often escalates fear. Acknowledge it, explain why general web pages mislead for his age group, and agree a concrete plan to replace searching.
Intimate symptoms are often delayed or described vaguely. Normalising early makes the history possible.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for the genital examination and record the offer and the response.

professional.t: Avoid unnecessary PSA testing in a low-risk young man: a false-positive result creates anxiety and further tests. Where PSA is considered, counsel about its benefits and limits first (GOV.UK PCRMP).
Examination of the genitalia needs a face-to-face appointment. Arrange it rather than relying on history alone.

community.t: Local sexual health clinics offer confidential STI testing and partner notification; he can self-refer if he prefers.

redFlags: Testicular lump or change in shape
Weight loss, bone pain or fever
psychosocial: Health anxiety and lost sleep from online searching
Sexual health context, asked without judgement
ice: Idea: blood in semen means prostate cancer
Concern: cancer; can’t sleep or stop thinking about it
Expectation: a straight answer on whether it is cancer

playbook.diagnosis: “In a man of 33 with no other symptoms, blood in the semen is almost always harmless and settles by itself. I’d like a few simple checks so we can be confident.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s a bit like a nosebleed in the plumbing: a tiny blood vessel along the way leaks for a while and then heals. It looks alarming because of where it is, not because of what it usually means.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you’ve convinced yourself it’s cancer and haven’t slept for days. At your age and with no other symptoms, that’s very unlikely, and I’ll check properly so you can trust that.”
management.psychosocial: Replace late-night searching with a concrete plan and a results call; offer the chance to talk again if anxiety persists.
sharedPlan: Urine dip and MSU; first-void urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
Blood pressure check and in-person genital examination (chaperone offered)
Treat any infection found; otherwise watchful waiting
PSA and DRE only if symptoms persist or new features appear
safetyNet: Return if persistent or recurrent, blood in urine, testicular lump or pain, fever or feeling unwell
Same-day care for urinary retention or high fever

pitfalls.intro: The trap in this station is swinging to one extreme: dismissing it without assessment, or over-investigating a low-risk young man. The marks sit in proportion, honesty, and clear thresholds.

items.fail: Reassuring without asking about haematuria, testicular lumps or systemic symptoms.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” Reassurance has to be earned by the history.
items.fix: Screen quickly and out loud: urine, testicles, fever, weight, bleeding.

items.fail: Requesting PSA and a suspected cancer referral for a 33-year-old with no red flags.
items.why: NICE NG12 PSA thresholds start at 40; a false-positive causes harm. Over-investigation is not “safe”.
items.fix: “A prostate test isn’t needed at your age unless something else turns up.”

items.fail: Saying “let me have a look” on a video call.
items.why: A genital examination can’t be done remotely; it needs a face-to-face visit with a chaperone offer.
items.fix: Arrange the examination and BP in person.

items.fail: Ignoring the embarrassment and diving into questions.
items.why: He is less likely to answer intimate questions honestly.
items.fix: “There’s nothing embarrassing about it. It’s a common reason to see a GP.”

items.fail: “The internet is always wrong” without explaining why.
items.why: Dismissing his research leaves the fear intact.
items.fix: “The websites mix up age groups. Prostate cancer is a concern mainly in older men with other signs.”

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the thresholds: persistence over weeks, blood in urine, lump, fever, and same-day care for retention.

NICE NG12 [1]: refer on a suspected cancer pathway if PSA is above the age-specific reference range (40–49 above 2.5, 50–59 above 3.5, 60–69 above 4.5, 70–79 above 6.5 µg/L; clinical judgement under 40) or the prostate feels malignant on DRE. GOV.UK PCRMP [3]: no ejaculation or vigorous exercise in the 48 hours before the test, and not within 6 weeks of a prostate biopsy; defer if there is active urinary infection.

NICE NG12 [1]: visible haematuria at 45 or over, or non-visible haematuria at 60 or over with dysuria or a raised white cell count, triggers the bladder or kidney route. A non-painful testicular swelling or change in shape or texture triggers the testicular route.

Treat a confirmed STI per the relevant BASHH guideline (for example the BASHH chlamydia guideline, 2026) and arrange partner notification. If symptoms suggest acute prostatitis, NICE NG110 [4] applies. Otherwise no treatment is needed; most episodes resolve without intervention.

Persistent or recurrent haematospermia, associated haematuria, abnormal prostate or raised age-specific PSA, a testicular lump, or systemic features: refer to urology (suspected cancer pathway where NICE NG12 criteria are met).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy; open question; let him describe the episodes and the fear in his own words.
Impact on sleep and anxiety; sexual health context asked without judgement.

Tests before reassurance is final; treat any infection; no routine PSA or imaging.
Anxiety and sleep addressed; STI contact tracing if positive.
Clear thresholds for return (persistence, haematuria, lump, fever, age), same-day advice for retention or sepsis, results call.

social.t: Late-night searching often escalates fear. Acknowledge it, explain why general web pages mislead for his age group, and agree a concrete plan to replace searching.
Intimate symptoms are often delayed or described vaguely. Normalising early makes the history possible.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for the genital examination and record the offer and the response.

professional.t: Avoid unnecessary PSA testing in a low-risk young man: a false-positive result creates anxiety and further tests. Where PSA is considered, counsel about its benefits and limits first (GOV.UK PCRMP).
Examination of the genitalia needs a face-to-face appointment. Arrange it rather than relying on history alone.

community.t: Local sexual health clinics offer confidential STI testing and partner notification; he can self-refer if he prefers.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “In a man of 33 with no other symptoms, blood in the semen is almost always harmless and settles by itself. I’d like a few simple checks so we can be confident.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s a bit like a nosebleed in the plumbing: a tiny blood vessel along the way leaks for a while and then heals. It looks alarming because of where it is, not because of what it usually means.”

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap in this station is swinging to one extreme: dismissing it without assessment, or over-investigating a low-risk young man. The marks sit in proportion, honesty, and clear thresholds.

items.fail: Reassuring without asking about haematuria, testicular lumps or systemic symptoms.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” Reassurance has to be earned by the history.
items.fix: Screen quickly and out loud: urine, testicles, fever, weight, bleeding.

items.fail: Requesting PSA and a suspected cancer referral for a 33-year-old with no red flags.
items.why: NICE NG12 PSA thresholds start at 40; a false-positive causes harm. Over-investigation is not “safe”.
items.fix: “A prostate test isn’t needed at your age unless something else turns up.”

items.fail: Saying “let me have a look” on a video call.
items.why: A genital examination can’t be done remotely; it needs a face-to-face visit with a chaperone offer.
items.fix: Arrange the examination and BP in person.

items.fail: Ignoring the embarrassment and diving into questions.
items.why: He is less likely to answer intimate questions honestly.
items.fix: “There’s nothing embarrassing about it. It’s a common reason to see a GP.”

items.fail: “The internet is always wrong” without explaining why.
items.why: Dismissing his research leaves the fear intact.
items.fix: “The websites mix up age groups. Prostate cancer is a concern mainly in older men with other signs.”

items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the thresholds: persistence over weeks, blood in urine, lump, fever, and same-day care for retention.
